messages.subject: Availability varies with distance - gdistsamp
parts:
Hello all,

I have been using gdistsamp to analyse survey data for a nocturnal, burrow-nesting species. I have found that models using data truncated to different distances give very different predictions of total population size. The more the data are truncated, the larger the population prediction. The structure of the top model is consistent across differently truncated data sets and GOF is good in each case. We are wondering whether the study system is just not suited to this type of model.

The species is not visible by day but vocalisations can be elicited by playing a recording of its call. We used point distance sampling, where an observer played the call at the central point and recorded the number of responses in each distance band. Not all individuals will respond on every occasion, and we have treated response rate as the availability part of the model. If an individual responds it is 'available' for detection. However, both response rate and detection probability are expected to decline with increasing distance from the observer.

I am struggling to get my head around whether the detection function part of the model will 'mop up' this possible decline in availability over distance. If not, is there another method I can use to account for this variation? Could this be the cause of the varying population estimates I get when including different distance bands?

Any advice would be much appreciated. I am happy to provide more information if needed.

Thanks,

Zoe

messages.author: 02d195331194f5bd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Availability varies with distance - gdistsamp
parts:
Confounding availability with distance is a problem. First, it pretty much ensures that the average availability varies across sites. Some sites will happen to more burrows close to the survey point, and therefore will have a higher average (over the whole site) availability, while other sites will happen to have more burrows further away from the survey point, and therefore will have lower average availability. The variation in availability across sites is a problem because the model that unmarked fits with gdistsamp uses data from all the sites to estimate availability in the same way that point count estimates use data from all the sites to estimate a constant detection probability. We know that violation of the assumption of constant detection probability in the point-count models can bias estimates pretty badly, so violation of the assumption of constant availability in the gdistsamp model is a pretty big concern. Second, even if the model were able to accurately estimate availability from the replicate surveys, the estimate of detectability will be biased low (and hence the abundance estimate biased high) because of the overlap between availability and detectability with regards to distance. 

However, if it's sensible to assume that "availability" is very nearly 1 at a distance of 0 (i.e. the animal will vocalize if you play the recording at the entrance to its burrow and the observer will hear it), then you can simply analyze the data in a standard distance sampling context with the "detectability" defined as the composite probability that an individual vocalizes and the observer hears it. You'd still want to watch out for large differences among predicted abundances if you truncate the data a bit or use different detection functions. 

If still possible, it may be better to conduct the surveys a little differently. 
  • Option 1 (a little more field work, & more modeling effort): try to estimate availability independently. You could do this by setting up speakers at varying distances from burrows, playing calls, and observing (from right next to the borrow) whether or not the animal responds. In this scenario, "availability" is defined as the animal vocalizing, and "detectability" is defined as your ability to hear the vocalization. Once you have an estimate of availability, you could fit a model where the probability of observing any given individual in each distance bin is the combination of availability (a known value at that distance) * detectability (an estimated value at that distance).
  • Option 2: if it's sensible to assume that a given occupied burrow is always occupied by the same individual, I think it would be worthwhile identifying the individual burrow that each call comes from and then analyzing in a mark-recapture framework. 
  • Option 3: use transect-based distance-sampling surveys to look for the burrows themselves and model burrow densities. Then get an independent estimate of burrow occupancy and adjust estimates of burrow density accordingly. 

Philip Shirk

messages.subject: Re: Availability varies with distance - gdistsamp
parts:
Hi Zoe,

-Does the sampling consist of one visit to each point with multiple time intervals, or multiple visits to each point? If the former, I have a little trouble wrapping my head around the meaning of the dynamics--I guess M_i is the population around the point during the visit and N_i,t is the subset that calls within a given interval? I guess this makes sense if you count each individual during each interval in which it calls. 

--If the data are structured such that your count by band only includes individuals in the first occasion in which they call, I think you would get positive bias, and it might make sense to sum these counts and use distsamp.

--Re. distance-related heterogeneity in availability, I think the model should be robust to this. I believe one of the simulation studies in Chandler et al. 2011 deals with this (in the context of movement rather than call rate, but same idea, I think). I think if phi is some half-normal function and p is some half normal function, you can still estimate of N/M by treating phi as a constant and p as a half-normal, but the sigma estimate for p will be much smaller than p's 'true' sigma. In other words, the product of two HN's can look a lot like the product of a binomial constant and an HN with a distinct smaller sigma. A quick sanity check (script at bottom) suggests so. The CI coverage may be permissive, however.  

-Re. phi~response rate: I don't think I would use a covariate derived from the observations to model variation in the observations.


John


###script
###z is distance
set.seed(8675309)
z<-rep(1:30, 50) ###say, 50 sites with 30 distance bands each
sigma1<-4 ##decay for putative phi
sigma2<-7 ##decay for putative p
p1<-exp(-z^2/(2*sigma1^2)) ##HN decay for phi
p2<-exp(-z^2/(2*sigma2^2)) ##HN decay for p
y<-rbinom(1500, 50, p1*p2) ##data--say we know each distance band at each site has 50 animals

###mis-specified likelihood--assumne phi is constant, and p decays HN
fx<-function(starts){
  i.phi<-starts[1]
  lsig<-starts[2]
  phi<-inv.logit(i.phi)
  sigma<-exp(lsig)
  p2est<-exp(-z^2/(2*sigma^2))
  ll<-sum(dbinom(y, 50, p2est*phi, log=TRUE)) 
  return(-1*ll)
}

###fit it
fit<-nlm(fx, p=c(0, 2))

print(c(inv.logit(fit$estimate[1]), exp(fit$estimate[2])))
###Note estimates are 'wrong'

###extract estimates of phi and p HN function
phiest<-inv.logit(fit$estimate[1])
p2est<-exp(-z^2/(2*exp(fit$estimate[2])^2))

###plot the true function underlying the observations
plot(z, p1*p2)

###plot the true function underlying the observations
points(z, phiest*p2est, pch=18)
###Note, it doesn't really matter
